Abstract
Reproducibility across diverse high-performance computing (HPC) environments remains a major challenge in computational
science, particularly for complex, multi-physics simulation workﬂows. This study presents a comprehensive approach to
achieving bit-for-bit result reproducibility in the context of the OpenGeoSys (OGS) simulation suite. Given the widespread
useofOGSinenvironmentalscienceapplicationssuchassafetyassessmentsforradioactivewastedisposalandtheoptimisation
of geothermal energy systems our approach enhances the reliability, transparency, and acceptance of simulation results in
these safety-critical domains, shown in a case study for far-ﬁeld deep geological repository assessment. We use GNU Guix
to deﬁne fully declarative, veriﬁable software environments and deploy them as portable Apptainer containers, enabling
consistent execution across multiple HPC systems. Leveraging AiiDA for workﬂow automation and provenance tracking, we
conduct simulations and complex simulation workﬂows on three heterogeneous clusters, conﬁrming identical binary-level
outputs. The results demonstrate that reproducible and portable software environments can offer a pathway toward long-term
veriﬁability in scientiﬁc high-performance computing. We also show how full data provenance originating from software
source code and model input data resulting in full simulation workﬂow result data can be achieved.
Introduction
Reproducibility is a cornerstone of scientiﬁc computing,
as it ensures that independent researchers can validate and
build upon previous results. For this study we deﬁne repro-
ducibility in scientiﬁc computing according to Essawy et al.
(2020) so that a researcher "is able to reproduce the analysis
in their own computational environment ... using the same
data, computational models, and methods, and code; ...". In
computational science, reproducibility is not just a matter
of scientiﬁc rigour but a practical necessity for verifying
that observed outcomes are not artefacts of speciﬁc hard-
ware, software, or conﬁguration choices. This is especially
true in high-performance computing (HPC) environments,

OGS uses the ﬁnite element method (FEM) to solve par-
tial differential equations (PDE) and its developers aim for
deterministic numerical behaviour which is a prerequisite
for result data reproducibility. We take some considerations
regarding numerical stability and deterministic algorithms
into account for the reproducibility study in Section “Repro-
ducibility study” and expect that simulation results (in the
scope of the chosen examples, see Section “Description of
conducted tests”) are invariant across machines, as long as
the software environment is identical (see Section “Deter-
ministic OGS builds”).
From the reasons given in Ivie and Thain (2018) why
computing should be reproducible we want to enable the
community of OGS users and developers to be able to "ver-
ify (or disprove) others results" of simulations and analyses,
especially crucial for applications in safety assessment and
to "survive the technology evolution", i.e. to be able to repro-
duce results in the future on different computing hardware
and environments.
In this paper we describe measures to ensure that OGS
simulations and workﬂows can be re-executed, at best even
years later, on different machines producing bit-for-bit iden-
tical results while still preserving the possibility to prove
the used binaries by recompilation from source to the exact
same binaries and thereby improving on certain causes of
"Reproducibility Debt" as described in Hassan et al. (2025).
We test our approach by reproducing the results of complex
simulation workﬂows for far-ﬁeld deep geological repository
assessment across heterogeneous HPC environments.
Methods
To ensure end-to-end (i.e. from input data, software environ-
ment, and deﬁned computing steps to results) reproducibility
of complex simulation workﬂows across heterogeneous HPC
systems, our study combines reproducible software envi-
ronments with automated data provenance (Simmhan et al.
2005) tracking of the workﬂow execution. We leverage the
functional package manager GNU Guix2 (Courtés 2013)
(hereafter referred to as Guix) to build bit-for-bit identical
software stacks from source, ensuring binary veriﬁability
and long-term reusability, and the AiiDA3 (Huber et al. 2020;
Uhrin et al. 2021) workﬂow manager to orchestrate and track
workﬂows across multiple computing environments. This
setup enables the practical deployment of reproducible sim-

Reproducible software environments with GNU Guix
Reproducible scientiﬁc computing in HPC environments
requires a stable software environment which is compat-
ible with the current hardware. On typical HPC systems
the user has limited control over the hardware and software
environments. Hardware may change due to replacement of
components like the upgrade of compute nodes for faster
computation or software environments change due to updates
of software packages, compiler, compiler ﬂags or Message
Passing Interface4 (MPI) variants. Typically, speciﬁc soft-
ware environments are supported only for a limited time,
after which they are replaced by newer software stacks.
Containerisation technologies such as Docker5 and, in
particular, Apptainer6 (formerly Singularity7, Kurtzer et al.
(2017)), have seen widespread adoption in HPC to enable
user-deﬁned software environments (Tesser and Borin 2023).
Containers are also frequently proposed as a solution for
creating reproducible software environments (Nüst et al.
2020; Polton et al. 2023; Zhou et al. 2023). However, they
typically encapsulate software in opaque binary bundles
that cannot be rebuilt or veriﬁed from source. This limi-
tation arises because container image deﬁnitions (e.g. via
Dockerﬁles) often depend on external package repositories
(Cheng et al. 2022), which are mutable and may become
unavailable over time (Courtés 2021). Other approaches to
software reproducibility require at least a compatible build
environment (Koch et al. 2021). Ensuring long-term repro-
ducibility and stability of computing environments remains a
major challenge in scientiﬁc computing. As shown by Vallet
et al. (2022), fully declarative speciﬁcations of all transitive
dependencies, including compilers and runtime libraries, are
essential to address this challenge effectively.
In this study we focus on reproducible software environ-
ments (builds) and their portable deployment to different
computing systems as a precondition for reproducible sim-
ulation runs. We address these challenges by using GNU
Guix, a functional package manager and source-based soft-
ware deployment system designed for reproducibility which
is based on the build and deployment layer of Nix (Dolstra
et al. 2004). Guix encourages bit-for-bit reproducible builds
by treating package builds as pure functions: each package is
deﬁned by its full dependency graph, which includes not only
direct dependencies but also the build environment, compiler

Guix allows to recreate speciﬁc software environments

their dependencies, and used compilers to a speciﬁc point
in time (i.e. to speciﬁc commits of the package deﬁnitions)

To deploy Guix-built software on non-Guix systems, such
as shared HPC clusters, we use the guix pack com-
mand to generate Apptainer container images and relocatable
tarball bundles. This approach allows us to distribute high-
performance (Xavier et al. 2013; Xie et al. 2018) software
environments, without requiring Guix to be installed on the
target systems. Combined with the guix time-machine
command, this mechanism provides a robust foundation for
the long-term veriﬁability and reproducibility of speciﬁc
simulation environments. The retrieval of package source
code is backed by Guix’ integration with the Software
Heritage8 archive (Cosmo and Zacchiroli 2017; Courtés
2019a, 2024), ensuring long-term availability of build inputs.
Together with Guix’ capability for full-source bootstrapping
(Nieuwenhuizen and Courtés 2023) and commit authentica-
tion (Courtés 2022a), these features establish a technically
sound foundation for reproducible and veriﬁable software
environments.

provenance model ensures that the entire study workﬂow

for OpenGeoSys and their deployment
with GNU Guix
To enable reproducible builds of OGS with Guix, we restruc-

we deployed bit-for-bit reproducible OGS builds including

Deploying OGS with Guix on non-Guix systems
Guix provides several mechanisms to deploy Guix-created
software (including all its runtime dependencies) on systems
where Guix is not installed (e.g. HPC environments):
– Generation of Apptainer container images via guix
pack -f squashfs
– Creation of relocatable binary archives using guix pack
-RR
– Generation of Docker images with guix pack -f
docker (not evaluated in this study)
In this study, we used the Apptainer container image
format for software deployment, as all target environments
supported container execution. SquashFS14 images used by
Apptainer bundle the entire software stack into a single ﬁle,
offering a convenient and portable deployment format. In
contrast, relocatable binary archives require extraction prior
to use, potentially resulting in a large number of individual
ﬁles which can be problematic on HPC systems with strict
inode (ﬁle count) limits. Docker image generation was not
tested, as none of the evaluated HPC platforms supported
native Docker execution.

Deterministic builds of dependencies
Unfortunately, container images produced on different mac-
hines were initially not identical due to the fact that they
include not only the requested software but all its at runtime
required Guix packages. While the OGS package has only 26
direct dependencies, these transitively pull in over 800 other
Guix packages. Some of these dependencies were found to
produce non-reproducible build outputs.
To diagnose such issues, we used diffoscope (Lamb
2025), a tool that recursively unpacks and analyses var-
ious archive and binary formats to highlight differences
in a human-readable form. It revealed sources of non-
determinism such as unstable input ordering and build
environment variations embedded in artifacts (Lamb and
Zacchiroli 2022; Reproducible Builds 2025). The repro-
ducibility issues identiﬁed were subsequently addressed
through contributions to the affected Guix packages, as sum-
marised in Table 2.
In addition to the runtime dependencies of OGS the bash-
package needs to be added to the container. We also added
the coreutils package to facilitate container inspection
and the intel-mpi-benchmarks package for conduct-
ing MPI performance tests. In total, the resulting container
includes 162 runtime packages, all of which can be built bit-
for-bit reproducible on different machines, from low-level
compilers up to the application layer, entirely from source
(Nieuwenhuizen and Courtés 2023).
To guarantee source-based builds, we used a clean Guix
environment (i.e. an empty Guix store15) and disabled
binary substitutes by building with the guix build --no
-substitutes ﬂag. When binary substitutes are enabled,
Guix queries designated substitute servers to check whether
a prebuilt version of each requested package is available. If
found, the compiled binary is downloaded instead of building
the package locally.

Container size reduction and performance improvements
Since the container image includes all runtime dependencies,
its size can be substantial. In the initial iteration the image
exceeded 1 GB. By stripping unnecessary build-time depen-
dencies, particularly from the PETSc runtime package (also
called "closure"), the container size was reduced to approxi-
mately 730 MB.
As OGS relies on PETSc for solving systems of equations
in parallel computations, it is essential for the simulation
performance to optimise PETSc for the target CPU archi-
tecture. Initially, it was observed that the Guix PETSc
package did not disable debugging by default, which neg-
atively impacts runtime performance. This was resolved by
addingtheconﬁgurationoption --with-debugging=0tothe
PETSc package deﬁnition.
Furthermore, Guix supports micro-architecture-speciﬁc
optimisation via the guix build --tune=[cpu architec
ture] option, which forwards the appropriate -march ﬂag
to the compiler (Courtés 2022b). The PETSc package was
modiﬁed to support tuning, and a tuning-related build ﬁx was
applied to the HYPRE library which is a PETSc dependency.
Finally a ﬁx in guix pack squashfs image generation was
required for successful PETSc test runs using the mpirun
command.

Reproducibility study
As shown in Fig. 1 this reproducibility study driven by an
AiiDA-based workﬂow contains two parts, ﬁrst it gener-
ates the software environment as described in the previous
section on three Linux server machines with different hard-
ware (2x AMD EPYC 9374F with 768 GB RAM, 1x AMD
EPYC9384Xwith1024GBRAM16)fromasourcebootstrap
(Nieuwenhuizen and Courtés 2023), compares the environ-
ments for identity and deploys it to the three HPC systems
shortly described in Section “Short description of HPC envi-
ronments”. Then it runs multiple tests on these environments
with increasing computational and numerical complexity and
compares the result data between the HPC environments for
identity.
In addition to workﬂow execution and data provenance
tracking, AiiDA manages the transfer of input data to remote
build machines and HPC environments, and collects results
and metadata from computational steps back to the devel-
oper’s machine. The complete workﬂow execution data from
this study is archived on Materials Cloud (Bilke et al. 2025),
a platform dedicated to sharing AiiDA workﬂow data. Each
workﬂow step, along with its input and output data, is identi-
ﬁed by a node ID. Instructions for examining the archived
data are provided in Appendix B. For efﬁciency, large simu-
lation output ﬁles are tracked using AiiDA’s RemoteData
type, which stores only a symbolic reference to the remote
folder rather than its full contents. A separate supplementary
data archive containing the full simulation outputs is avail-
able at (Bilke 2025a).
Short description of HPC environments

The following considerations regarding numerical stability
and algorithmic determinism were essential in selecting the
test cases presented in this study.
Numerical stability is a property of the underlying PDE
system. In the FEM context, stability is generally ensured
as long as certain conditions are met, such as well-posed
PDEs, appropriate boundary conditions, acceptable levels of
anisotropy, and moderate nonlinearity. The study comprises
of problems with growing numerical difﬁculty, from a sim-

In contrast, algorithmic determinism refers to the prop-
erty that identical input always produces identical output.
OGS avoids constructs which use external state, such as ran-
dom number generators with non-ﬁxed seeds to eliminate
this potential source of non-determinism. Another common
source is out-of-order execution, which can arise in parallel
computations. For example, a seemingly simple operation
like summing the entries of a vector can lead to different
numerical results depending on the order of summation due
to ﬂoating-point cancellation effects. On a single thread or
MPI rank, such operations are typically performed left-to-
right and are thus deterministic. However, in a multi-threaded
or multi-rank setting, the order of partial summations is not
guaranteed. Depending on how partial results are merged,
different rounding paths may lead to slight variations in the
ﬁnalresult.Furthermore,linearsystemsolversmayintroduce
additional sources of non-determinism. For instance, solvers
that use pivoting strategies, such as MUMPS, may yield dif-
ferentresultsdependingonthedomaindecomposition.While
different partitionings can lead to different pivot choices, for
a ﬁxed partitioning the solver is expected to behave deter-
ministically.
OGS uses PETSc for parallel computation which has some
measures in place to enable deterministic behaviour of par-
allel computations such as phased assembly of vector and
matrix operations and we used non-pivoting solvers only.
Effects arising from OpenMP (shared-memory) parallelisa-
tion were not analysed in this study because shared-memory
parallelisation does not scale beyond a single compute node,
while our simulations may be required to run on multiple
nodes (e.g. because of memory or run time requirements).
OpenMP parallelisation in OGS currently only affects the
solver and, for some processes, the assembly step whereas
the full MPI-based parallelisation with PETSc also includes
parallel input and output operations and therefore scale
better even beyond a single compute node. Furthermore,
hybrid parallelisation (Rabenseifner et al. 2009), combining
distributed-memory (MPI) with shared-memory (OpenMP)
parallelization strategies, is not yet implemented in OGS.

Simulation runs
OGS can be build in a serial and a parallel version. The par-
allel version uses the distributed memory approach based on
the MPI standard. Hybrid-parallelisation (Rinaldi et al. 2022)
is possible too but was not used in this study. In a parallel
simulation multiple cores are used to compute a solution. On
each core an OGS instance is executed, processing only the
local sub-domain it is responsible for. For the contribution to
the solution on the global domain communication between
the particular OGS instances is needed. Consequently, a pre-
requisite is the decomposition of the computational domain
into sub-domains. In the left panel of Fig. 2 such a decom-
position is depicted. For the parallel solving of equations
the PETSc library (Balay et al. 1997) is used, that offers a
variety of linear solver implementations. Furthermore, data
structures to handle matrices and vectors offered by PETSc
are also used in the parallel version.

Workﬂow runs
To evaluate the reproducibility and portability of complex
scientiﬁc workﬂows in a realistic setting, we selected the
AREHS project (Carl et al. 2023) as a representative use case.
Unlike simpliﬁed test cases, The AREHS project models
real-world simulation scenarios (Zill et al. 2024b; Silber-
mann et al. 2025) relevant to long-term safety assessments
of deep geological repositories.
AREHS workﬂow description The AREHS project investi-
gates the impact of changing external boundary conditions on
hydrogeologically relevant parameters of a potential geolog-
ical repository site in Germany. Particular emphasis is placed
on the effects of glacial loading and unloading cycles, which
induce mechanical stress changes and temperature varia-
tions resulting from permafrost formation and subsequent
warming periods. The associated workﬂow encompasses
all essential and automatable steps, from geological model
preparation to OpenGeoSys simulations and the generation
of result diagrams (for an example see Fig. 4). The workﬂow
is executed using the Snakemake workﬂow manager, which
organises the computational steps into a directed acyclic
graph (DAG), as illustrated in Fig. 3.
Packaging workﬂow tools with Guix The AREHS work-
ﬂow uses a speciﬁc build conﬁguration of OGS which uses
optimised parallel solvers from the Intel MKL library17 in
combination with PETSc. This speciﬁc PETSc variant was
contributed as a new Guix package petsc-openmpi-mkl
(Bilke 2025b) to the guix-science-nonfree channel as the
ofﬁcial Guix channel has the strict requirement of pro-
viding free software only whereas the Intel MKL is dis-
tributed under a proprietary license. The Python-based
Guix packages python-ogstools (Zill et al. 2024a),
python-ogs6py and python-vtuinterface (Buch-
waldetal.2021),python-glaciationBCs(Silbermann
2023), and python-papermill (Seal et al. 2023) have
been added to the guix-ogs channel.
Unfortunately, bit-for-bit reproducibility could not be
achieved for all contents of the AREHS workﬂow container.
Speciﬁcally, the build system of the python-scipy pack-
age embeds timestamps into its compiled library ﬁles, and sev-
eral texlive-* packages also produce non-reproducible
outputs due to timestamp-related issues, a known problem
tracked in Guix issue #73613 (Cournoyer 2024). Embedded
build timestamps in package binaries is a common repro-
ducibility issue (Malka et al. 2025) but they are unlikely to
affect the runtime behaviour or numerical correctness of the
software.

Snakemake, executes independent workﬂow steps in par-
allel across all available cores of a single HPC node with
embedded parallel simulations (using 8 cores each) using
the container MPI-implementation only (see Listing 4).

Conclusions
We have shown that our approach to reproducible and
portable software environments successfully enables the bit-
for-bit reproduction of results in the scope of the chosen
examples.WiththisworkweenhancedtheOpenGeoSyssoft-
ware package by addressing several key categories of issues
that contribute to "Reproducibility Debt" according to Has-
san et al. (2025), p. 11ff. We resolved Missing dependencies
for complex software systems (ID 4.1) and Version upgrada-
tion in programming languages, libraries, operating systems,
and other dependencies (ID 5.1) by pinning the whole depen-
dency graph with Guix and relying on the integration of Guix
and the Software Heritage archive for bit-for-bit reproduc-
tion of the software environment. By using the same software
environment which runs in a portable way on all tested sys-
tems we mitigated Inconsistent software/hardware settings in
different computing environments (ID 4.2), at least within the
scope of the tested computing environments. This study may
outline required steps and common challenges also for other
(geoscientiﬁc) simulation software projects aiming to enable
reproducible builds and improve result reproducibility on
HPC environments. This study also adheres to the FAIR prin-
ciples (Wilkinson et al. 2016): All software environments,
workﬂow deﬁnitions, and simulation artefacts have been
archived with persistent identiﬁers and are openly accessible
via platforms such as Materials Cloud and Software Her-
itage, ensuring long-term ﬁndability and availability. The use
of standardised, declarative tools like GNU Guix and work-
ﬂow systems such as AiiDA and Snakemake ensures that the
computational processes are both interoperable across HPC

Achieving bit-for-bit reproducibility of computations is
feasible only when all computational steps are identical.
When variations such as different solver conﬁgurations or
domain decompositions (e.g. number of partitions) are intro-
duced, result comparisons must rely on more ﬂexible metrics
than SHA1 checksums. For such cases, tools like vtkdiff
(Naumov et al. 2025) allow comparisons of simulation output
meshes using absolute or relative error norms. In the con-
text of computations on regular workstations investigating
reproducibility of shared-memory parallelized simulations
(which employ different solver conﬁgurations as distributed-
memory parallelized simulations) e.g. comparing a regular
OpenMP runtime with Deterministic OpenMP (Aviram and
Ford 2011) is an interesting future research topic. Looking
ahead, reproducibility may be challenged by the rapid shift
toward GPU-based architectures (Hoffmann et al. 2022),
which may not support the same instruction sets as current
CPUs. This raises important questions about the replicabil-
ity of results (as deﬁned in National Academies of Sciences,
Engineering, and Medicine (2019): "Obtaining consistent
results across studies aimed at answering the same scien-
tiﬁc question with new data", although we see the changed
software environment as new data too), especially when
future systems differ signiﬁcantly in hardware or require
software stacks compiled for new computing architectures.
Our approach, based on Guix, offers a promising foundation
to explore such replicability questions in evolving compu-
tational landscapes, including the impact of updated Guix
software stacks or newer releases of OpenGeoSys.

Abstract: Reproducibility across diverse high-performance computing (HPC) environments remains a major challenge in computational science, particularly for complex, multi-physics simulation workﬂows. This study presents a comprehensive approach to achieving bit-for-bit result reproducibility in the context of the OpenGeoSys (OGS) simulation suite. Given the widespread useofOGSinenvironmentalscienceapplicationssuchassafetyassessmentsforradioactivewastedisposalandtheoptimisation of geothermal energy systems our approach enhances the reliability, transparency, and acceptance of simulation results in these safety-critical domains, shown in a case study for far-ﬁeld deep geological repository assessment. We use GNU Guix to deﬁne fully declarative, veriﬁable software environments and deploy them as portable Apptainer containers, enabling consistent execution across multiple HPC systems. Leveraging AiiDA for workﬂow automation and provenance tracking, we conduct simulations and complex simulation workﬂows on three heterogeneous clusters, conﬁrming identical binary-level outputs. The results demonstrate that reproducible and portable software environments can offer a pathway toward long-term veriﬁability in scientiﬁc high-performance computing. We also show how full data provenance originating from software source code and model input data resulting in full simulation workﬂow result data can be achieved.
